newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank, ECB cannot override forex markets.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank, ECB cannot override forex markets.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, lambasting the idea that the future European Central Bank could set out to steer currency rates, said on Monday that central banks could not simply override market forces.
In a speech at an institute in Freiburg, Germany, Tietmeyer said, "Neither the Bundesbank today nor the European Central Bank tomorrow can steer the exchange rate against the judgment of markets".

Attacking the idea that it could be desirable for the Bundesbank to pay greater attention to the external exchange rate of the mark in its policies, Tietmeyer said that such an idea had only come about because inflation tensions were low.
"This idea is certainly also a reaction to the current high level of price stability," he said.

Tietmeyer's comments fall against a background of calls, from some French politicians in particular, for a specific exchange rate policy to be followed alongside monetary policy once Europe creates a single currency in 1999.
Such calls are anathema to the German central bank, which views price stability as the absolute priority but sees a strong currency as a key element in the pursuit of this goal.
Tietmeyer also rejected the view that, even if the central bank detached itself from exchange rate targeting, politicians should follow this policy instead.

"There is a view that politicians should dictate the exchange rate," Tietmeyer said according to a text released in advance. "And if the exchange rate, contrary to expectations, does not allow itself to be set by politics then (the view goes) there must be something wrong with the markets."

But he added that this view, which had been problematic even in the late 1950s, was illusory in the age of global financial markets, which set exchange rates in line with their expectations of the credibility of policies.
"A central bank cannot vary this level of credibility by a few percentage points at will," Tietmeyer said. "It either has credibility...or it does not."
A low external currency rate could certainly be bought at the expense of non-credible monetary policy, but the price for this was domestic inflation, he said.

"In the longer term there is an inextricable link (between external stablility) and inner stability," Tietmeyer said. "A euro which is internally stable cannot be weak externally and vice versa. No one can make the circle into a square."
